newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Aid chiefs appeal for help to reach Zaire refugees.
newsitem.headline: Aid chiefs appeal for help to reach Zaire refugees.

text.p: Aid agencies appealed to the world on Saturday to urgently help them get aid to hundreds of thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees on the run in eastern Zaire.
Support for a planned multinational task force in east Zaire has cooled after the return home to Rwanda of 500,000 Rwandan Hutus fleeing a Tutsi revolt in the region.
But the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, Sadako Ogata, said the force was still needed to help agencies find up to 700,000 wandering refugees in eastern Zaire.

"We have no access," Ogata told reporters during a one-day Geneva meeting on the crisis in central Africa, chaired by Canada and attended by top Western and U.S. humanitarian officials and heads of relief agencies.
"I think the international community and those who have the capacity to move in with various advanced modern technology would probably be able to give us access," she said.
Ethnic Tutsi guerrillas have seized large swathes of eastern Zaire in a lightning rebellion and are blocking aid agencies from going deeper into Zaire to look for the lost refugees.
Prospective troop-contributing nations met in Stuttgart, Germany, for a second day to decide whether there was a need for an armed intervention force to bring aid to the region.

The Geneva meeting, also attended by French State Secretary for Humanitarian Affairs Xavier Emmanuelli and U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) chief Brian Atwood, was called as the thrust of relief efforts moved to Rwanda after the mass return home of Hutus.

It remained unclear how a consensus would be reached amid questions over priority aid areas, confusion over the number of refugees and wavering among many countries over plans for a multinational task force.

High on the agenda for Rwanda, which faces the daunting task of resettling the refugees in Africa's most crowded country and which opposes the deployment of an international force in east Zaire, was a request for $700 million in extra aid.

"We have made an assessment of needs for speedy resettlement and reintegration of refugees. We need around $700 million," Charles Murigande, head of Rwanda's government delegation and transport and telecommunications minister, told reporters.
"The main elements are emergency need for food and quick assistance. But housing is the major aspect."
And confusion surrounded the questions of how many refugees needed help and where they were.
Ogata said UNHCR had field information that up to 700,000 refugees were still on the run in east Zaire.

On Friday, Canada's Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril, whose country is coordinating the U.N.-authorised multinational mission plans, told a news conference in Stuttgart estimates of refugees in east Zaire varied from 100,000 to 400,000.
USAID chief Atwood told Reuters that the U.S. estimate was for around 400,000.
A senior official of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) urged Tutsi rebels, Rwandan government officials and Zairean authorities to cooperate with aid agencies.
The Hutu refugees fled to east Zaire in fear of retribution for the 1994 Hutu-led genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda, after which a Tutsi-dominated army swept to power in Rwanda.

"There is a lack of cooperation by the parties involved, including the so-called rebels. We also need the cooperation of Zairean as well as Rwandan authorities," the Geneva-based ICRC's head of operations, Jean de Courten, told reporters.
"There are many arguments on the numbers. But this is not the problem. The problem is that there are people victimised in eastern Zaire. The priority for ICRC is access to these people."
